lead: A change of variables turns a hard region into an easy one. The Jacobian is a single number, built from first partial derivatives, that records how much that change stretches area or volume at a point. It is the determinant of the matrix of partials, with rows for the new variables and columns for the old. Engineers use it to switch a double integral to polar coordinates, to convert between coordinate frames in robotics, and to track how small errors grow through a chain of measurements.
prereq: You need: partial derivatives from Chapter 4.2 and 2×2 and 3×3 determinants from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Definition: a determinant of first partials

blocks.text: Take two old variables x and y and two new ones u = u(x, y), v = v(x, y). Write u<sub>x</sub> for ∂u/∂x, and so on. The Jacobian is the determinant of the 2×2 array of first partials, with one row per new variable and one column per old variable.
∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = det [ u<sub>x</sub>  u<sub>y</sub> ; v<sub>x</sub>  v<sub>y</sub> ] = u<sub>x</sub>v<sub>y</sub> − u<sub>y</sub>v<sub>x</sub>
blocks.where: u and v are the new variables; x and y are the old ones; u<sub>x</sub> = ∂u/∂x, and so on; det means determinant.

blocks.text: For three new variables u, v, w in three old ones x, y, z, the array is 3×3 and you expand it along any row. Some syllabi call the number the Jacobian determinant and the matrix alone the Jacobian matrix.
∂(u, v, w)/∂(x, y, z) = det [ u<sub>x</sub> u<sub>y</sub> u<sub>z</sub> ; v<sub>x</sub> v<sub>y</sub> v<sub>z</sub> ; w<sub>x</sub> w<sub>y</sub> w<sub>z</sub> ]
blocks.where: each row is one new variable; each column is one old variable.

items: The notation ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) reads “u, v with respect to x, y”.
Rows are the new variables; columns are the old ones.
Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant.
The determinant is unchanged if you swap rows with columns, because a matrix and its transpose have the same determinant.
Differentiate each new variable with respect to each old variable.
Place u<sub>x</sub>, u<sub>y</sub> in the first row and v<sub>x</sub>, v<sub>y</sub> in the second row.
Expand the determinant using u<sub>x</sub>v<sub>y</sub> − u<sub>y</sub>v<sub>x</sub>.
For three variables, expand the 3×3 determinant along a row with easy zeros.

sections.h3: Three properties that do the work

blocks.text: The chain rule multiplies Jacobians. If u and v depend on s and t, and s and t depend on x and y, the overall Jacobian is the product of the two Jacobians in the order written.

blocks.where: u, v depend on the intermediate variables s, t; s, t depend on the original variables x, y.

blocks.text: The inverse rule says a map and its inverse have reciprocal Jacobians. Do not confuse the inverse map with the transpose: ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) is 1 divided by ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y), not the same number.

blocks.where: the map is one-to-one and its Jacobian is not zero.

blocks.text: The third property is the useful test. J = 0 exactly where the map loses independence, that is, where u and v are functionally related. For example, u = x + y and v = 2x + 2y give fu<sub>x</sub>v<sub>y</sub> − u<sub>y</sub>v<sub>x</sub> = (1)(2) − (1)(2) = 0, and indeed v = 2u. Only a few universities prove the general statement; in an exam you use it as a test. A nonzero Jacobian means the map is locally invertible near that point.

sections.h3: Standard Jacobians and change of variables

blocks.text: Three Jacobians come up so often that you should carry them in memory. Here ρ is the distance from the z-axis in cylindrical coordinates, and in spherical coordinates ρ is the distance from the origin, φ is the angle from the positive z-axis, and θ is the angle in the xy-plane.

head: Coordinates
Transformation
Jacobian
rows: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ
x = ρ cos φ, y = ρ sin φ, z = z
x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ

blocks.text: For polar coordinates the check is short: x<sub>r</sub> = cos θ, x<sub>θ</sub> = −r sin θ, y<sub>r</sub> = sin θ, y<sub>θ</sub> = r cos θ. The determinant is r cos²θ + r sin²θ = r. So a small rectangle in the (r, θ) plane has area r dr dθ in the (x, y) plane.

In a double integral, dx dy becomes |J| dr dθ when you change to coordinates (r, θ). The absolute value is there because area is positive; the sign of J records orientation, which the limits can absorb. For polar coordinates, dx dy = r dr dθ, and the extra r is exactly why polar integrals are easier for circles. The integration itself belongs to Unit 5, change of variables.

examples.question: For u = x² − y² and v = 2xy, find ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) at (x, y) = (1, 2). Then find ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) at the image point and verify the inverse rule.
steps: At (x, y) = (1, 2): u<sub>x</sub> = 2, u<sub>y</sub> = −4, v<sub>x</sub> = 4, v<sub>y</sub> = 2.
Product: 20 × 0.05 = 1, so the inverse rule holds.
examples.check:
x = 1.0
y = 2.0
ux = 2*x
uy = -2*y
vx = 2*y
vy = 2*x
J = ux*vy - uy*vx
print(J)
print(1/J)
print(J*(1/J))

traps: Swapping the two rows changes the sign of the determinant, so fix an order: new variables down the rows, old variables across the columns.
Do not write ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) as the transpose of the matrix. The determinant of the transpose is the same, but the inverse Jacobian is the reciprocal 1/J.
Sign slips in the 2×2 expansion are common: the formula has a minus between u<sub>x</sub>v<sub>y</sub> and u<sub>y</sub>v<sub>x</sub>.
In an area integral use |J|. Forgetting the absolute value gives a negative area when the map reverses orientation.
J = 0 is a dependence test, not a statement that the functions are constant. u = x + y and v = 2x + 2y have J = 0 but neither u nor v is constant.

quiz.a: ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = det [ u<sub>x</sub> u<sub>y</sub> ; v<sub>x</sub> v<sub>y</sub> ] = u<sub>x</sub>v<sub>y</sub> − u<sub>y</sub>v<sub>x</sub>.

quiz.q: Give the Jacobian for spherical coordinates.
quiz.a: ρ² sin φ, where ρ is the distance from the origin and φ is the angle from the positive z-axis.

quiz.q: Why does ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) equal 1 divided by ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)?
quiz.a: The map from (x, y) to (u, v) and the inverse map from (u, v) to (x, y) compose to the identity. The chain rule gives J × J′ = 1, so the inverse Jacobian is the reciprocal.

quiz.q: Find ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) for u = x + 2y and v = 3x − y.
For x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, compute ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ).
quiz.a: x<sub>r</sub> = cos θ, x<sub>θ</sub> = −r sin θ, y<sub>r</sub> = sin θ, y<sub>θ</sub> = r cos θ. J = r cos²θ + r sin²θ = r.

quiz.q: For u = x + y and v = 2x + 2y, compute J and explain what J = 0 says about the map.
quiz.a: u<sub>x</sub> = 1, u<sub>y</sub> = 1, v<sub>x</sub> = 2, v<sub>y</sub> = 2, so J = 2 − 2 = 0. Also v = 2u, so u and v are functionally related; the map does not give two independent new variables.

quiz.q: A map has J = 0 at one point and J ≠ 0 nearby. What does that tell you about the map at the point?
quiz.a: The map is not locally invertible at that point; a small region is collapsed in one direction. It does not mean u and v are dependent everywhere, only that the independence fails at that point.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Jacobian matrix is the derivative of a vector map, and its determinant is the local volume scale. The full matrix drives Newton–Raphson for systems of equations, finite element meshes use a positive Jacobian to keep elements from turning inside out, and robot control maps joint speeds to hand speeds with a Jacobian. Search for “Jacobian matrix robotics”, “inverse function theorem” and “change of variables multiple integrals”.
